column2: One of the two matters had been settled. The other had to begin with Ji Heling. “Mr Xuexuan,” Hu asked directly, “what has happened about Heling?” Wang lowered the glass he had almost raised to his lips and sighed dispiritedly. “It has been keeping me awake at night. I was waiting to discuss it with you. I don’t know what the governor intends. It looks very much as though he means to destroy the bridge after crossing the river. How can I face Brother Heling?” He described his successive approaches to Huang Zonghan. He had first made a request; when no definite answer came, he had submitted a recommendation. That too had achieved nothing, so he had argued the case forcefully. Still there had been no result. “Xueyan, you judge these things more accurately than anyone. What do you make of it?” “There is no death without a ghost at work,” Hu said bluntly. “There must be something underhand behind this.” “I thought so too. I asked the men handling the correspondence whether some little inducement was needed. They answered quite sincerely that everything depended on the governor. They did not dare accept anything yet, for fear of taking a favor and then failing to accomplish the business. Once Mr Ji’s appointment order was issued, of course, they would expect him to treat them to a celebratory drink. Xueyan, surely that says all there is to say?”

Comparing Wang’s account with Ji’s, Hu understood at once. The two thousand taels were wanted by Huang Zonghan, who was unwilling to have Wang supply them. That explained these answers. If the money were merely for the correspondence staff, why would they care whether it belonged to Wang or Ji, so long as the silver was good? Hu understood, but would not reveal it. If he did, Wang would still feel guilty that he had failed to do enough for Ji, even if he paid. And Ji, having declared that he would not buy an office, might bring the whole affair to an impasse. Hu therefore smiled. “Let them play their ghostly tricks. I am a Maoshan Taoist who specializes in catching such ghosts. Just watch me!” “And how do you intend to catch them?” Wang asked. “Heaven’s secrets must not be disclosed.” Hu pointed to Ji. “Mr Xuexuan, in his letter Heling mentioned that the tribute rice would go out to sea through Liuhe. Because the Small Swords uprising might cause trouble, he suggested a plan. See what you think of it.” Ji was astonished. When had he suggested any plan? He was about to speak when someone gave him a light kick. Recognizing Hu’s signal, he remained silent.

“What plan?” Wang asked attentively. “Our superiors are worrying about it, and it is giving me a headache too. Escorting tribute grain is a public duty, yet the troops make demands at every turn. The whole Green Standard Army ought to be abolished!” “Then this suggestion will be useful,” Hu said calmly. “Heling knows my friendship with You Laowu and the extent of You’s influence. His idea is to contract the transshipment to You. What do you think?” Wang considered, then struck the table in approval. “A splendid idea! You belongs to the Songjiang grain-transport brotherhood, so the benefit would not go to outsiders. It can be justified on every side. Brother Heling, you truly have remarkable talent. Please draw up a memorandum today, and I’ll present it to the governor in person tomorrow. If he still raises objections, there really must be a ghost at work!” “Certainly, certainly,” Ji replied. His face and ears grew hot, though the wine concealed his embarrassment. “Excellent!” Wang raised his glass. “I have drunk brandy several times, but none seemed as fragrant or mellow as this.” “‘Friendship with Zhou Gongjin is like drinking mellow wine,’” Ji quoted from the Records of the Three Kingdoms. He raised his glass toward Wang, but his eyes rested on Hu. After they drank, Wang said, “That is enough wine. Brother Heling still has his memorandum to write tonight. Come to my house tomorrow evening, and we’ll enjoy a proper drink.”

As he finished, Ruiyun lifted the curtain and came out smiling. “But I haven’t yet offered a toast to Master Hu or to you, sir.” “You certainly ought to toast Master Hu—to thank your matchmaker!” That had indeed been her intention, but Wang’s saying it aloud made things difficult. With the wine pot in one hand and a cup in the other, she stood awkwardly at a loss. It lasted only a moment before Ji came cleverly to her rescue. “Mr Xuexuan should be toasted first,” he said, taking the pot. “Xueyan and I are brothers. He is one of the family.” “How unfortunate!” Wang laughed. “You are all family, and I’m the only outsider.” “You mustn’t say that, sir.” Ruiyun recovered her composure and her skill in social conversation. “Neither Master Hu nor Master Ji regards you as an outsider.” “Exactly!” A little wine had sharpened Wang’s wit. “A woman’s heart turns toward her husband. It is you who regard me as an outsider.” “I would never dare.” Though he was joking, she answered seriously. “I spent more than ten years in your household. I could never forget your kindness and your wife’s.” Even with wine as an excuse, Wang could hardly continue teasing after that. He accepted her toast with proper courtesy. She then toasted Hu and put down the cup to leave, but Hu stopped her and insisted she toast Ji as well. Now she could not remain at ease. The more she demurred, the more Hu teased, until several children gathered behind the curtain to peep at the fun. Danhe, the most mischievous, giggled incessantly. By turning to scold his children, Ji gave Ruiyun another opportunity to escape.

After dinner they returned to the study for tea and resumed their business. “Have you discussed the transshipment with You?” Wang asked Hu. “We have discussed it, but nothing is settled. I did not know your wishes.” “You might just as well have decided yourself. What does You say?” “One word is enough with him. The cost can be negotiated; he only needs an official communication from Zhejiang to the Jiangsu grain transport circuit intendant.” “The document is easily arranged. Even a letter to Governor Xu of Jiangsu would be no trouble. But we need an approximate figure for the expense before we can plan.” “I imagine it will be much cheaper than having Green Standard troops provide an escort.” “Then that will do.” Wang considered carefully. “If You can truly guarantee its safety, this is an excellent arrangement.” Hu heard the uncertainty about You. There were many things he could not conveniently explain, such as You’s friendship with Zhou Lichun. Yet Wang’s concern, and the fact that the proposal was now being attributed to Ji, made reconsideration necessary. If something went wrong, it would jeopardize both men’s careers. “I am reasonably confident, but we must guard against the one chance in ten thousand,” Hu said, looking at Ji. “Perhaps the memorial should leave some room for maneuver and let Governor Huang decide.” “No, no!” Wang waved his hand. “He will not take the responsibility.”

The whole matter seemed to require fresh discussion. Hu felt the responsibility was too heavy for any plan to be entirely secure. While he was pondering, Ji spoke. “We must first circle the horse and bend the bow—prepare the ground before acting. Defense is pressing everywhere, and every locality needs more troops. The existing forces are already insufficient. How could men be spared to escort the tribute rice?” “Ah!” Wang exclaimed. “I understand.” “So do I,” Hu said. “But it would be better if those words did not come from you, Mr Xuexuan.” “You mean the Green Standard officers should say it themselves?” Wang shook his head. “They won’t. It is a comfortable and profitable assignment. Why would they refuse?” “Not necessarily comfortable. If they really encounter the Small Swords forces and have to fight, they will be no match for them.” “Unfortunately, they do not think so, and I cannot say it. I’ll see the governor myself and act as circumstances require.” “What about the memorandum?” “Have it drafted tonight all the same. I’ll take it with me. Better to have it ready and not need it than need it and not have it.” “Then I’ll finish it tonight,” Ji said. After a pause, he added, “I should like Xueyan to stay so that we can discuss it and make it as sound as possible. What do you think?” “Very well.” Wang looked at Hu. “We shall meet tomorrow morning, then.”

With that agreed, Wang took his leave. Hu and Ji began immediately. One arranged the arguments clearly; the other wrote fluently. They soon produced a draft, reconsidered it, settled the final wording and made a fair copy for Hu to take away. The next morning Wang stayed home especially to await Hu. As soon as he arrived, they shut themselves in the study. Since the Xincheng disturbances had been put down, Wang had gained still more of Huang’s confidence. That also meant more jealous rivals and more obstruction. He had many troubles to pour out to Hu. “Xueyan, there is an important matter I want to discuss. I hear that Governor Huang may be transferred. If he leaves, who knows what his successor will be like? I am strongly tempted to withdraw while things are going well.” Hu was greatly alarmed. “Mr Xuexuan, why should you think of that? We have only just built things up, and everything is running smoothly. Why retreat now?” “First, if the new man and I do not get on, winding up the affairs I have handled could become troublesome. It would be easier to hand them over while Governor Huang is here. Second, Jiang Zhongyuan has been promoted from judicial commissioner of Hubei to governor of Anhui. We are old acquaintances, and he has written to ask whether I would join him there. He and Zeng Guofan are both enjoying great imperial favor. Going to him might be a good move.” “I disagree!” Hu shook his head vigorously. “You do not know Anhui, and neither do I. To speak plainly, if you go there, I shall not go with you, because I could do nothing to help you there.” “Very well.” Wang nodded. “Since you put it that way, there is no more to say. I will write today to decline Jiang’s kind invitation.”

Hu was naturally reassured, but felt his responsibility grow heavier. After reflecting, he asked, “Is the report of Governor Huang’s transfer reliable?” “There is such a rumor, and we must be prepared. Besides, disturbances by bandits are occurring throughout Zhejiang. A spark can set the prairie ablaze. The governor takes the matter very seriously. Because the Xincheng affair was handled well, I fear all these assignments will fall to me in future. Meanwhile I cannot get free of the Sea Transport Bureau. I really am beginning to lack the strength for everything.” This made Ji’s appointment all the more important. In truth, Wang was more anxious about it than Ji himself, but he could not exert his full influence with Huang. In allocating the rewards for Xincheng, Wang had made a wrong move—or rather, failed to make a move at all. Huang had decided from the outset that Wang and Ji would receive one confidential recommendation and one open recommendation between them. He had no preference as to which man received which. Had Wang said when the report went forward, “Ji Heling did more of the work; please favor him with the confidential recommendation,” Huang would have agreed. Because Wang had failed to say this, the confidential recommendation had gone to him. To press Ji’s claims again now might look opportunistic, and he feared displeasing Huang. That was why he had never dared say too much. He could hardly confess this difficulty even to Hu. As time passed, his sense of guilt, almost as though he had appropriated another man’s merit, deepened. He longed for Hu to devise a way to settle the appointment quickly. “As things stand,” Wang continued, “it will probably take more than a day or two. I must first discuss defense and make the governor see that no troops can be spared. Then I must wait for him to ask whether there is another way. Only then can I produce Heling’s memorandum. Think how many turns we have to take!”

Hu agreed. Reviewing the causes and consequences once more, he realized that he had been mistaken. He had wanted Ji to display his abilities. But the memorandum had little bearing on whether Ji could take over the Sea Transport Bureau. The decisive point still lay with the correspondence office. A pig’s head cooks when the fire is brought to it; official business proceeds when the money arrives. How had he forgotten such familiar sayings? “Mr Xuexuan, please wait a little. See the governor tomorrow at the earliest, or the day after at the latest.” “Why? What are you arranging now?” “The same answer as before.” Hu smiled. “Heaven’s secrets must not be disclosed.” “Very well. I won’t ask. I’ll wait for your word.” They went on to talk about events in Shanghai and Hangzhou. There was too much to finish at once, especially when Mrs Wang came out to entertain their guest and the subject turned to Ruiyun. Hu put business aside for a while and joined in the conversation. He stayed for lunch, then went straight to Fukang to attend to Ji’s affairs.

Using his own bank’s notes, he made out two: one for two thousand taels and one for two hundred. He sealed them in an envelope, inscribed it “A humble gift,” and signed beneath, “Your humble junior, Ji Heling.” “Qingsheng, I must ask you to make a visit. Have Master Liu Er pass this to Master Chen in the correspondence office. Say that I shall be busy for a few more days, but once these miscellaneous affairs are settled, I should like him to come over for a talk.” “Very well. Should I ask for a card acknowledging receipt?” “No. If he gives you one, bring it back. If not, there is no need to request it. The intention will be understood.” Liu Qingsheng was quick. Within a double-hour he returned with a visiting card from Master Chen, a correspondence officer at the governor’s office. On it were four characters: “Gratefully received, with thanks.” That night Hu notified Wang that he could now see the governor about the matter. Wang had no idea what Hu had done, but was sure that following his advice would not lead him astray. The following day he dressed formally and went to the governor’s office. After his calling document was taken in, Liu Er returned. “His Excellency says he has many visitors this morning. He asks that you come at three this afternoon.” When a superior set aside a specific time for consultation, it was a sign of special regard: he meant to allow an unhurried discussion. Wang therefore went home and returned in the afternoon.

Huang received him in the Boat Hall in the rear garden of the governor’s residence. He first asked Wang to change into informal clothes, then invited him to share refreshments: layered cake, yanpi soup, water-chestnut cakes, sweet and savory dishes, hot and cold—all flavors of their native Fujian. As they ate, they discussed the situation. Huang began with Xiang Rong’s Jiangnan Grand Camp, which consumed enormous sums every month. Its official demands for money arrived with the urgency of a fire alarm and never ceased. It was a severe headache. “Zhejiang should not have to provide everything,” Wang offered. “The demands are endless and cannot be sustained. Might you discuss an overall arrangement with Commander Xiang? Jiangsu, Jiangxi and Zhejiang could each be assigned a fixed monthly sum, to be remitted when due. That would make it easier for everyone to raise the funds.” “A good suggestion. I can try it,” Huang said. “Your work in Huzhou is particularly important. The province depends chiefly on that district for military funds. I think the Sea Transport Bureau is indeed more than you can also manage.”

Wang grew uneasy. From this remark, it sounded as though the governor already had someone in mind. If he named the man now, with superior and subordinate face to face and no room for an intermediary, would Ji not lose his chance? Worse still, another man’s arrival would require an immediate handover. Unless money could be found to cover the deficit at the Sea Transport Bureau, the shortage would be exposed. That would be disastrous. Sweat appeared on Wang’s forehead. Unaware of the cause, Huang said, “This little spring in the tenth month is very warm. Please remove your hat.” To do so in a superior’s presence was discourteous. Wang wiped his brow with a handkerchief. “It’s quite all right.” Huang did not insist over a small matter and returned to business. “That fellow Ji seems to have some ability.” At these words Wang felt his heart lighten and his senses clear. “Your Excellency has a discerning eye. No true talent can escape your notice.” The compliment was well judged, and Huang’s lean face broke into a smile. “Let him take over your work at the Sea Transport Bureau,” he said as though seeking advice. “What do you think?” “Nothing could be more suitable. Ji Heling’s ability is of the first order. Some call him too proud, but I do not entirely agree. Talented men may be proud of their gifts, yet their scorn is directed at those inferior to themselves. He understands very well how he ought to behave. If Your Excellency gives him an important appointment, I guarantee that he will repay the favor and give you complete satisfaction.” The last words implied more than competent public service. Huang did not really need Wang’s guarantee: Hu’s Fukang banknote carried greater force. He nodded. “I know. Go back and prepare to hand over.”

“Yes, sir!” Wang rose and made a formal obeisance. “Your Excellency’s allowing me some relief from my burden is a great kindness.” “Not at all. Please rise.” Huang stood too and made a gesture of assistance. Remaining on his feet signaled that he was ready to see his visitor out. “I shall take my leave,” Wang said, adding a final sentence to make the matter firm. “I will tell Mr Ji at once of Your Excellency’s gracious encouragement and ask him to serve you wholeheartedly.” “You may tell him. I will have the appointment order issued immediately.”

Wang’s first act on returning home was to send for Hu and Ji. Naturally, Hu arrived first. Fukang was nearby, and he had already told Wang’s gate attendants to look for him there whenever needed. “Wonderful, wonderful!” Wang said, raising his thumb. “Xueyan, what miraculous powers do you possess, to judge events so exactly?” He recounted the interview in detail. Hu had not expected such smooth success either and was delighted. After a moment he asked, “What happened about the memorandum?” “I did not present it. Producing it would have made us seem to have planned everything beforehand. There are two kinds of great men. One likes others to anticipate his wishes and think everything through for him. The other likes to exercise an unpredictable authority and does not want anyone to know his mind. Governor Huang is the second kind. I thought it better for Heling to make the request himself after taking office, or when he goes to thank the governor for the appointment.” “It must be done quickly. Let him raise it when he gives thanks. And the papers for transporting the guns?” “Ah, I forgot about those. Never mind—a letter from me will do.” He had just finished writing when Ji arrived. Wang and Hu congratulated him and briefly explained what had happened. Ji could not quite grasp the sequence or tell whose influence had brought it about, so he thanked them both. The male and female servants of the Wang household came to kowtow and offer congratulations. Ji happened to have a thirty-tael note with him and generously gave it as a reward to be shared among them. Some said Ruiyun should be congratulated too and praised her good fortune. The two maids awaiting marriage were particularly envious of her rise from a lowly perch to the station of a phoenix. Their admiration showed in every word and expression. Hu felt almost as pleased as Ji himself. After this happy bustle, Wang said, “Brother Heling, you had better go home. Messengers with congratulations may already be there. Xueyan, go with him and help attend to matters. We will talk again tonight.”

By helping attend to matters, Wang meant seeing to the customary rewards. Hu did not know the going rates very well, so he first asked Wang for details. Then he stopped at Fukang to leave instructions before accompanying Ji home. “Second Brother,” Ji said directly when they arrived, having thought it through in the sedan chair, “did you work through someone?” Because Ji had declared that he would not buy an office, Hu answered discreetly. “I merely asked someone to put in a word.” “What sort of word?” “Only a request for help.” Ji reflected in silence. “I won’t ask further. I understand in my heart.” Just then Liu Qingsheng arrived, carrying what Hu had instructed him to bring: a thousand-tael banknote, five hundred taels in silver, and a passbook showing another three thousand five hundred. Holding the passbook, Ji said, “Second Brother, this weighs heavily on me. I can scarcely bear it.” He meant that he owed more kindness than he feared he could repay. “We are brothers. Why say such things?” Hu replied. “Water helps the boat, and the boat helps the water. There will be plenty of occasions when I must depend on you.” “That goes without saying. Your business is mine. I do not yet know the inner workings of the Sea Transport Bureau. I shall need your help to manage it.”

Their conversation was interrupted by a servant showing in a visitor, a goshha from the governor’s office. The Manchu word originally meant attendance or service, then came to denote a guard; later it was used for the officers who ran errands for governors and governors-general. This man wore a gold hat finial and held the eighth rank. But before Ji, an expectant magistrate of the seventh rank, he dared not stand on his own official status. He hurried forward and made two formal salutations. “Congratulations, Master Ji!” He had plainly come with the good news. Ji modestly disclaimed the honor, helped him up and asked his surname. “My unworthy surname is Zhu. The governor assigned me to the correspondence office. Master Chen sent me especially to congratulate you.” From his document case he produced an appointment order bearing a large purple seal and offered it with both hands. The envelope was unsealed. Ji took out the order and read it: he was indeed to succeed Wang as executive director of the Sea Transport Bureau. He passed it to Hu and turned back to Zhu. “Thank you for your trouble. Please sit down.” “I would not presume. Master Chen asked me to congratulate you first and to say that he will call this evening. He also said the governor is not feeling quite well today. You need not go to thank him for the appointment until tomorrow.” “Very well. Please tell Master Chen how deeply grateful I am for his attention. I shall certainly visit his residence this evening.” “Yes, sir. May I have your visiting card to report completion of my errand?”

This had already been prepared: a visiting card and a red envelope containing twenty taels. As soon as Zhu had been sent off, Ruiyun appeared in a lined purple satin jacket and a pale violet silk skirt, with a red flower in her hair. Smiling, she said, “Master Ji, I have come to congratulate you.” “What is this?” Ji was surprised and a little flustered. “Must you observe these formalities too? There is no need. Please don’t.” “It is only proper. My warmest congratulations, Master Ji.” Resting a hand at her left waist, she made a formal curtsy, then called, “Danhe, bring your brothers and sisters to kowtow to your father.” Danhe led the children out from behind the door, pushing and jostling. Ruiyun had clearly arranged it all beforehand. Dressed as neatly as for New Year, they stumbled onto a long felt mat, laughing as they bowed. Ji helped one up and gathered another into his arms, while trying to answer mischievous Danhe’s demands for a reward. The confusion and merriment could hardly have been greater. When it subsided, Ji said, “Ruiyun, we really must thank Second Master.” “Yes,” she interjected, “but it isn’t merely thanks we owe him. We should congratulate him too.” “Congratulations all round! Two joys at one door, and no end of celebratory wine!” Hu laughed. “Ruiyun, you brought all this good fortune.” The compliment filled her with delight. She could not help glancing at Ji, then composed her expression. “We shall be busy for several days. Well-wishers will arrive soon, so tea, tobacco and refreshments must be prepared. Please make yourself comfortable, Second Master. I must leave you.” She curtsied again and withdrew.

The bearing of a woman from a great household required composure: a noiseless step and a skirt whose folds did not stir were considered signs of good fortune. To Hu’s surprise, Ruiyun already possessed this manner. She had probably long meant to emulate the mistress she had served. Her ambition was evident, and he could not help exclaiming, “Very good indeed!” Ji too had noticed how completely she looked the part of an official’s lady, and was naturally pleased. His thoughts wandered back to his first meeting with Hu two months before. It seemed like a dream—an intoxicating spring dream from which he would not soon wake, with still more delightful scenes ahead. His boundless happiness turned into deep reflection. “It is really rather amusing,” he said. “On the day we first met, I complained that you and Mr Xuexuan had laid a trap: one I could neither refuse nor willingly accept. Who would have thought it was a trap like this? Even the most uncompromising man might want to walk into it.” The memory made Hu still prouder. Since meeting Wang, he had devised many unusual schemes, but none pleased him more than winning over Ji Heling. First, it had saved Xincheng from the disaster of armed conflict. Second, it had greatly helped Wang. Third, it had allowed a worthy man to advance instead of lamenting that his talent went unrecognized. Fourth, it had brought about a happy match. Finally, Hu himself had gained a friend as close as flesh and blood. One action had achieved so many good things. He felt that his ingenuity had served him well. Half joking, he said, “You once told me how many extraordinary schemes Chen Ping devised for Emperor Gaozu of Han. I have plenty of schemes too, for great matters and small. Great talents can be put to great use and lesser talents to lesser use. It all depends on the person concerned.”

“Indeed,” Ji replied. “You ought to be the honored adviser of a great lord. Your present position does not do you justice.” “Not necessarily. Things depend on human effort.” Talking with Ji had unconsciously given Hu’s speech a literary flavor. “As the saying goes, generals and ministers are not born of a special breed; a man must strive for himself. I may not be a great lord’s honored adviser now, but if I help someone rise to that position, I shall naturally become one.” “Well said! Troubled times bring talent forward. History gives us example after example.” “I don’t know what the books say. But, Elder Brother,” Hu’s face took on a rare expression of sober seriousness, “I believe you when you say this is an age in which talent can rise. In troubled times, one need not be bound by seniority and established rules, so capable men have a better chance. There is something else. If you go to Shanghai and deal with foreigners, you will see that they have real strengths. Call them cunning if you like, or cold and lacking in loyalty. In one respect we cannot match them: they distinguish clearly between right and wrong. If you are right, they acknowledge it and admit their own mistake. We may know perfectly well that we are wrong and still refuse to admit it, as though doing so would cost our great celestial empire its dignity. When people recognize your merits as foreigners do, you have more energy for work and more chance to use your abilities. Talented people like to accomplish things; they are not necessarily thinking only of themselves. High office and generous pay alone may therefore produce no talent at all—only the ‘slaves’ that Bannermen call themselves before the emperor.” “Well!” Ji opened his eyes wide. “I never expected such a spirited argument from you. I may have read a few more books, but in knowledge of the world I cannot compare with you.” “I am only talking at random,” Hu said modestly. “My lack of reading remains a disadvantage.”

“Not at all, not at all.” Ji shook his head and changed the subject. “I told you that I wanted to meet some friends from the brotherhood world, You Laowu first among them. We shall certainly need his help now. After taking up my duties, I should like to visit Shanghai and Songjiang, both to inspect conditions at the sea outlet and to call on You in person. Could you come with me?” “Yes. I have many things to attend to in Shanghai myself. But it is too early to settle that. Let us discuss it after you have thanked the governor and taken office tomorrow.” At this point Zhang Gui announced a visitor bearing congratulations. It was Qiu Fengyan. After greeting the host, he turned to Hu with almost reverential admiration. Qiu had always admired Ji above others. That Hu could win over such a proud man of talent and go on to become his sworn brother seemed like the Buddha’s subduing the Monkey King. It could not fail to inspire awe. Hu was fond of Qiu too. The man was warmhearted, good-tempered and willing to take a loss. Most unusually, he could recognize the strengths of others and admire them sincerely. His tastes were distinctive. In some respects he was vulgar beyond description; yet he could do something so original and refined that it outdid the cultivated. That was one reason Ji was able to be his close friend. What Hu particularly liked was his lively spirit. Even if his family had no rice for the cooking pot, he looked as though he had eaten well, slept soundly and wanted only to enjoy himself.

Hu at once thought of a task suited to him. “Old Qiu, don’t go away today. Help our host entertain his visitors.” “A duty I cannot refuse!” Qiu replied cheerfully. “Brother Heling is riding the spring breeze, and his reputation is soaring. There will be plenty of callers; leave them all to me. I have plans for the celebration too—banquets and opera. We can have at least ten days of festivities.” “Wait, my dear fellow!” Ji hastily stopped him. “Spare me your schemes. You’ll make me look like a man who has suddenly come into money.” “Every office has its appropriate ceremony. Who doesn’t celebrate a little?” “What times are we living in? The Long-Haired rebels have fought their way north of the Yellow River, and the Small Swords have risen in Shanghai. If we make a senseless uproar here and one of the censors in Beijing hears of it, a passing mention in a memorial on public affairs could bring us more trouble than we could carry.” “That is true,” Hu agreed, recognizing the need for caution. “Old Qiu, there is no need for extravagance now. A quiet day or two among friends will mark the occasion well enough. In any case, there will be another celebration by the end of the year.” “Quite right!” Qiu readily accepted the better counsel. “Brother Heling, taking a concubine at year’s end will be as joyful as marriage, which people liken to success in the examinations. Surely you cannot then slight that lady of ours, so talented, beautiful, virtuous and kind?” “We shall see. If official business runs smoothly and I am free at the year’s end, a celebration would do no harm.” “Good! That is all I needed to hear. Naturally I shall be the master of arrangements then.”

“Of course. We shall have to trouble you. Are you busy at present, Old Qiu?” “You know me—busy with nothing.” “Then be busy with something useful.” Ji turned to Hu. “What do you think of asking Old Qiu to help?” “What objection could there be?” Then a thought struck Hu. “What sort of help do you have in mind?” “Escorting the shipments, naturally.” “That is what I thought.” Hu turned to Qiu. “Would you condescend to serve as a convoy commissioner for the Sea Transport Bureau?” “There is no question of condescending. I have never been on a sea-going vessel and don’t know whether I might be seasick. But never mind all that. Whatever you two decide, I’ll do.” “Much obliged!” Ji clasped his hands, then said to Hu, “I suspect you have another task for Old Qiu too.”

“Yes. Burn incense and visit the monk—two errands accomplished in one journey. Once your memorandum is approved, we can ask him to go to Songjiang first.” “I see! You want him to bring back the guns.” “Exactly. I had intended to send my young pupil. But he may be too young and inexperienced, and after all, a ‘first-rank commoner’ still cannot compare in standing with our distinguished Master Qiu.” “Enough, enough!” Qiu said in mock surrender. “Brother Xueyan, stop teasing me. You have talked for so long, and I still don’t quite understand the business.” Hu outlined the arrangements for transferring the tribute grain and buying guns from the British. Qiu loved activity and friendship. Like Ji, he was eager to meet a man such as You Laowu, and transporting foreign guns sounded new and interesting. He agreed without reservation. “But to speak frankly, the journey is not entirely without risk,” Ji warned. “Bandits are everywhere these days, and many secretly covet such effective weapons. You are famous as the Wine Muddlehead, Old Qiu. You must drink less on the way.” “I can drink a little less. Don’t worry. At every meal I always stop just short of becoming muddled.”

Ji and Hu laughed. “Old Qiu,” Hu asked curiously, “have you ever been drunk in your life?” “Only once. On my wedding day, and then deliberately.” “Why?” Hu asked in surprise. “Out of resentment. My late father arranged the marriage. I wanted to marry the girl next door, but he absolutely refused. I had a stubborn notion of my own: I could not stop the bridal chair from entering, but whether husband and wife shared a heart as well as a room was my affair. At the wedding feast, my young schoolfriends made a great commotion and pressed drinks on me. I refused none of them and was already six or seven parts drunk. When I entered the bridal chamber, instead of lifting the bride’s veil, I lifted the cover of a wine jar. I drank until I collapsed unconscious and slept a whole day and night before waking.” “You deserved a beating!” Hu said, laughing with curiosity. “The bride must have cried all night.” “She didn’t cry. My late mother did! She had never seen me drunk and was frightened. Do you know how drunk I was? It was the eleventh month, yet a piece of bean curd placed on my chest became burning hot in no time.”

“Good heavens!” Hu clicked his tongue. “You might have drunk yourself to death.” Ji had never heard this story. He was more interested in the bride and quickly asked, “What did your wife do? Even if she didn’t cry, she must have pleaded with you.” “Nothing of the kind!” Qiu shook his head. “You could guess until daybreak and never imagine what she did.” “Then spare us the guessing and confess the truth.” “She sent the woman attending her back to her parents’ house with a message: the new son-in-law loved wine as dearly as life itself, so they should send twenty jars of good wine.” “Wonderful!” Ji exclaimed. “And what did you do?” “What could I do? It is rare in life to find someone who understands you. I loved wine, and she found good wine for me. How could I fail to surrender?” Ji and Hu laughed heartily, and Qiu laughed too at the happy absurdity of his younger days. “Strange to say, from that day I saw my wife differently. Before, I had thought her so plump that she looked stupid. Now I reflected that Imperial Consort Yang was plump, Consort Wan of the Ming was plump, and Xue Baochai in Dream of the Red Chamber was plump too. Her feet were a little large, admittedly. Those three-inch golden lotuses of hers—” “Wait!” Ji interrupted. “How can three-inch golden lotuses be large feet?” “I hadn’t finished,” Qiu replied calmly. “My wife’s three-inch lotuses are measured across, like the feet of Guanyin herself.” Laughter erupted both inside and outside. The children might not understand his wit, but the adults’ merriment was contagious. Danhe had never seen her father and his guests laugh so uncontrollably; the spectacle itself struck her as comical, and she laughed harder than anyone. Ruiyun was already so full of happiness that laughter came readily. Besides, she understood Qiu’s wonderfully pointed description of his plump, large-footed wife.

Amid the laughter another distinguished visitor arrived: Wang Youling. The atmosphere naturally became more formal. With Qiu present, neither host nor guests could speak with much hidden meaning. Once congratulations and thanks had been exchanged, Wang said, “Brother Heling, everything is ready for my handover. You may take over at any time. Rather than choose a special day, why not use the opportunity at hand? After thanking the governor tomorrow, come to the bureau and begin your duties. Then I can lay down the burden and breathe a little more easily.” “Mr Xuexuan,” Ji replied apologetically, clasping his hands, “I am afraid I cannot comply in that respect. Please let me first consult you properly before taking over.” “Then…” Wang glanced at Qiu. “Brother Fengyan, will you join us for a simple dinner at my house?” Qiu was thoroughly versed in social affairs. He understood that the others had already arranged to meet and would have private matters to discuss. He must not make himself unwelcome, but he would not state the reason openly. “I’ll impose on you another day,” he said, pointing to the floor. “Brother Heling has charged me with receiving his well-wishers. Tonight I shall impose on his household for my wine.” That suited everyone. Ji went inside especially to tell Ruiyun to look after their guest. With apologies and thanks to Qiu for his trouble, he left with Wang and Hu.

At Wang’s house, Mrs Wang had ordered a banquet from the Xiaoyoutian Fujian restaurant, both to congratulate Ji and to welcome Hu home. However sumptuous the dishes, a banquet for only three would lack the company to make it enjoyable. Hu therefore proposed inviting some colleagues from the Sea Transport Bureau. It would let Wang thank them for their usual assistance and introduce them to Ji. Summoning guests with hurried invitations was not particularly courteous, but among colleagues it mattered little. While they waited, Wang took his visitors into the study to discuss the handover. There was a deficit in the bureau’s accounts. By long-standing custom, a successor generally inherited his predecessor’s deficit as an outstanding item. If he could cover it, he did; if not, he passed it on to his own successor. When it could no longer be passed on, serious trouble followed. Much depended on the predecessor’s influence, on whether the successor was accommodating or exacting, and on their relationship. Here the outgoing and incoming men were virtually one person, so no disagreement was expected. Hu nevertheless felt that a definite arrangement was necessary. Otherwise Ji would bear the burden, which would trouble Hu’s conscience; and any eventual scandal would only make trouble for Hu himself. “Mr Xuexuan,” he began, “this is like taking over a shop. Even brothers should keep clear accounts. The debt may remain outstanding, but its amount must be settled precisely. We can then decide how to clear it. Once my Shanghai silk is sold, I think there will be no difficulty.” Wang understood at once. “Of course. We share good fortune and bad. We cannot simply dump a ruined concern on Brother Heling.” That made matters easier. Whatever could be accounted for as expenditure would be so accounted for; whatever could not would remain outstanding, to be reconsidered if it could no longer be carried forward. With Hu there, Ji would not be left in difficulty. Their existing relationship with Fat Zhang would continue unchanged. Ji listened, nodding without speaking. That was the appropriate attitude. He owed the appointment to Wang and Hu; this was no time to advance his own demands. Once in office, he could exercise his abilities so long as he did not harm either of them. There was no need to assert himself now.

When they turned to staffing, however, Ji did have something to say. “Mr Xuexuan, which men at the bureau must be retained?” Wang understood. “I have no personal men there,” he replied, meaning none whose interests were closely bound to his own. “But one or two have worked hard. Keep them if you can. If you really find them unsuitable, of course it is for you to decide.” He named two colleagues. Ji noted their names and said he would do his best to retain them. “Is there anyone else you would like a place found for?” Wang considered. “A distant nephew has recently come from our native place. I do not want to take him to Huzhou, for fear people will say there are too many official relatives about. If you could place him, I should be most grateful.” “Certainly. Please have him give me an account of his qualifications. Xueyan and I have also agreed that we should like to employ Qiu Fengyan. What do you think?” This was Ji’s tact: he deliberately showed respect and cordiality. Even had Wang disapproved, he would scarcely have objected to an arrangement Hu supported. In fact, it did not concern his interests, and he thought well of Qiu. He nodded repeatedly. “Very good, very good.”

“There is another matter,” Hu added. “I should like Old Qiu to go to Songjiang and collect the foreign guns on the same journey. Please arrange another official document.” “The papers are easy. But will the Wine Muddlehead make a mistake on such an errand? I think it would be best to send that young fellow Chen with him. He is young, but capable.” “Since you think him capable, why not give him some appointment in Huzhou?” Hu said without thinking. Then, realizing that this was not quite what he wanted, he quickly added, “A nominal appointment, of course.” “Why a nominal one?” “There is a reason. Chen Shilong is to marry at the end of the year. An appointment would put him among men entitled to official dress and make a better showing for both families.” “That can be done,” Wang replied casually. “Whose family is the bride from?” “The bride is A’zhu.” “Ah!” Wang and Ji showed the same surprise and bewilderment, neither knowing how to pursue the question. They did not need to ask. Hu himself related how he had arranged the future of that fresh blossom from a humble home. Both listened closely, but their reactions differed. Wang felt regret on Hu’s behalf; Ji approved heartily, saying that this spirited act had the chivalrous generosity of a hero from a Tang tale.
